extracted.intended_audience: Citizens and voters of New York (readers considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution); delegates and public interested in constitutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Normative guidance and argumentative principles justifying federal powers over the militia and taxation in the proposed U.S. Constitution, addressed to citizens deciding on ratification. Presents standards for how powers should be allocated between national and state governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity in militia organization
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘uniformity in the organization and discipline of the militia would be attended with the most beneficial effects, whenever they were called into service for the public defense.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uniform organization and discipline enable militia to operate with mutual intelligence and concert, fit them sooner for proficiency in military functions, and are therefore desirable; such uniformity can only be accomplished by confiding regulation of the militia to the national authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional provision for militia regulation (textual standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plan proposes to empower the Union ‘to provide for organizing, arming, and disciplining the militia, and for governing such part of them as may be employed in the service of the United States, RESERVING TO THE STATES RESPECTIVELY THE APPOINTMENT OF THE OFFICERS, AND THE AUTHORITY OF TRAINING THE MILITIA ACCORDING TO THE DISCIPLINE PRESCRIBED BY CONGRESS.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This specific allocation—national regulation of organization/discipline and governance of federally-employed militia, with states retaining officer appointments and day-to-day training—balances uniformity with state influence and is presented as the proper constitutional arrangement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militia as substitute to avoid standing armies
rubrics_metrics.description: If the federal government can command the aid of the militia in emergencies, it can the better dispense with the employment of a standing army; to render an army unnecessary is a more certain method of preventing its existence than prohibitions on paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal control over militia reduces the inducement to create standing armies (viewed as dangerous to liberty); thus organizing militia under national authority is a safeguard against permanent military establishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to require citizen assistance (posse comitatus implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: A right to pass all laws NECESSARY AND PROPER to execute declared powers would include that of requiring the assistance of the citizens to the officers who may be intrusted with the execution of those laws (i.e., posse comitatus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rebuts the objection that absence of an explicit posse comitatus provision implies reliance only on military force; necessary-and-proper authority implies power to call citizen assistance when proper.

rubrics_metrics.name: State appointment of officers mitigates danger from select corps
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection: select corps of the young and ardent might be rendered subservient to arbitrary power. Counter: with the particular States to have the SOLE AND EXCLUSIVE APPOINTMENT OF THE OFFICERS, this circumstance will always secure to them a preponderating influence over the militia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because officers are appointed by states, fears that a federally-regulated militia would become an instrument of despotism are diminished; militia members' community ties further reduce risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticability of disciplining the entire populace; prefer select corps and periodic musters
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The project of disciplining all the militia of the United States is as futile as it would be injurious... To oblige the great body of the yeomanry ... to be under arms ... as often as might be necessary ... would be a real grievance to the people, and a serious public inconvenience and loss.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for having the people properly armed and equipped and assembling them once or twice a year, while forming ‘a select corps of moderate extent’ that is well-trained and ready; this is the practical substitute for a standing army and the best security against it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of country as security against usurpation
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The obstacles to usurpation and the facilities of resistance increase with the increased extent of the state... The natural strength of the people in a large community, in proportion to the artificial strength of the government, is greater than in a small...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large republic's size and diffusion of power make popular resistance more practicable and decrease likelihood of successful usurpation by national rulers; distant States can raise fresh forces to oppose local subjugation.

rubrics_metrics.name: State governments as mutual checks on national power
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The State governments will, in all possible contingencies, afford complete security against invasions of the public liberty by the national authority... The legislatures will have better means of information... they can at once adopt a regular plan of opposition...’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State legislatures, possessing information, civil organs, and popular confidence, can detect and check federal usurpation and coordinate resistance, and the people may ‘throw themselves into either scale’ to preserve liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: General power of taxation necessary to national purposes
rubrics_metrics.description: The federal government ought to possess the power of providing for the support of the national forces, the national civil list, payment of national debts, and, in general, for all matters which will call for disbursements out of the national treasury; therefore a general power of taxation must be interwoven in the frame of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Money is ‘the vital principle of the body politic’; without a complete power to procure a regular and adequate supply, government risks ‘continual plunder’ or decay. The national government must be able to raise revenue by ordinary taxation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: National taxation rather than requisitions on states
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliance on quotas and requisitions is a fallacious system; the substitute is permitting the national government to raise its own revenues by the ordinary methods of taxation authorized in every well-ordered constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience shows requisitions are unreliable and enfeeble the Union; permitting the federal government to tax directly avoids continual deficiencies and political friction between federal and state governments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of internal vs external taxation distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguishing INTERNAL and EXTERNAL taxation (reserving internal to states, external to federal) would ‘violate the maxim of good sense and sound policy, which dictates that every POWER ought to be in proportion to its OBJECT;’ commercial imposts alone would be insufficient for national needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxing power must be commensurate with the objects it must achieve; artificially limiting federal taxation to external duties would leave the national government dependent and weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means must be proportioned to ends; power commensurate with object
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘A government ought to contain in itself every power requisite to the full accomplishment of the objects committed to its care... every power ought to be commensurate with its object; that there ought to be no limitation of a power destined to effect a purpose which is itself incapable of limitation.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This axiom underpins the argument for unconfined national power where the national object (e.g., defense, peace) admits no practicable external limit; constitutional powers should therefore match necessary scope of duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: National taxation enables credit and borrowing in crises
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of creating new funds upon new objects of taxation would enable the national government to borrow as far as its necessities require; without it, creditors would distrust a government that depends on thirteen other governments for means of fulfilling contracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct taxing power secures public credit in wartime and allows the Union to avoid diverting appropriated funds (which would destroy credit); ability to raise revenue underpins international and domestic borrowing capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependence on requisitions leads to governmental atrophy and temporizing
rubrics_metrics.description: A government half supplied and always necessitous cannot fulfill its purposes; dependence on requisitions results in a succession of expedients temporizing, impotent, disgraceful, with frequent sacrifice of engagements to immediate necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political and administrative stability, dignity, credit, and ability to undertake enlightened public plans require reliable revenue streams—hence the necessity of national taxing authority rather than intermittent requisitions.
